problem: LLM-based statutory question answering fails temporally: post-cutoff staleness (models apply superseded provisions after amendments) and recency bias (models prefer newer provisions even when a historical version governs the fact pattern). Law evolves continuously while LLM knowledge is a static snapshot.
method: Benchmark of 312 expert-validated, time-sensitive German statutory QA pairs in three categories (Post-Cutoff Amendment, Pre-Amendment, Multi-Provision Pre-Amendment). Five LLMs evaluated under four settings: Vanilla, Web-search, RAG-kNN and RAG-ToC. Both RAG variants extract the "as-of" date from the query with a regex and use it as a hard constraint that filters the retrieval space to paragraph versions valid during that period, then retrieve by embedding (kNN) or via a statute table of contents (ToC).
key_assumptions: The query's applicable date can be recovered by a regex pattern over the question text
Legal validity should be enforced as a hard constraint rather than a soft relevance signal
German civil-law statutes and LLM-generated, expert-validated questions are representative of time-sensitive statutory QA
Version validity depends on effective/amendment dates, not on temporal proximity
main_contribution: A temporal legal benchmark for diagnosing post-cutoff staleness and recency bias, plus evidence that strict "as-of date" version filtering is the most effective mitigation ("treating temporal validity as a hard constraint").
datasets: Own benchmark: 312 expert-validated German statutory QA pairs (3 categories)
benchmarks: Own temporal statutory QA benchmark (Post-Cutoff Amendment, Pre-Amendment, Multi-Provision Pre-Amendment)
baselines: RAG-ToC (table-of-contents mediated retrieval over version-filtered corpus)
metrics: LLM-as-a-judge rubric score, validated against human expert ratings
results: Severe degradation in the Vanilla post-cutoff setting. Both RAG approaches substantially improve performance across all question types; web search yields unstable gains and shows marked recency bias on historically anchored tasks. The authors report no significant difference between RAG-kNN and RAG-ToC, inferring that the correct timeframe matters more than the retrieval method.
limitations: Single jurisdiction and language (German civil law)
Questions are LLM-synthesized and then expert-validated, so construction artifacts are possible
Hard filtering depends on a regex date extractor over query text
Only hard version filtering is tested; no soft/graded temporal re-ranking is evaluated
Retrieval-layer ranking metrics are not separately reported
future_work: Section 6 is titled 'Conclusion and Open Questions'; abstention mechanisms when queries exceed a model's temporal knowledge are suggested in Section 2.3 as safer alternatives to returning outdated legal conclusions
code_availability: Dataset published at https://github.com/TUMLegalTech/temporal_bias (repository exists; root files 'Prompts' and 'qa_set.xlsx'; README is empty, so the arXiv link is unconfirmed by the repo itself).

relation_to_idea.conceptual_difference: This work treats temporal validity as a hard, discrete constraint and targets LLM staleness/recency at answer time; the proposed idea instead re-ranks candidates with a continuous elapsed-time relevance term added to semantic similarity and claims retrieval-agnosticism. Crucially, this paper's conclusion that validity should be a hard constraint directly challenges the soft-decay premise.
relation_to_idea.basis: Both papers address time-sensitive statutory QA over amended provisions; this paper also supplies the benchmark and the hard-filter baseline that the proposed soft temporal score must beat. Method overlap is high but not full because it enforces validity by discrete interval filtering rather than a continuous elapsed-time term.
